6.11 Assuming new lignite-fired plants would be similar to the existing ones, the same stack gas emission problems that apply to northern coal also apply to Texas lignite, but to a greater extent. Similarly, lignite plants are base-load and do not operate efficiently to serve peaking demand. Lignite also produces large quantities of residue which must be returned to the open pit or buried. Lignite-fired steam electric generation is not a viable alternative to Amistad hydropower at this time because it is not efficient when used for peaking, because stack gas emission controls have not been developed satisfactorily, and because large quantities of residue require special handling. But, given the choice between Amistad hydropower and lignite-fired steam, particularly since the Amistad Dam and Reservoir are already in existence, the conclusion favors hydropower because it is less environmentally adverse. Again, the lignite power and the hydropower are most complimentary to each other.
6.12 Nuclear. There is no assurance that the nation's available supply of uranium is unlimited as was thought to be the case at one time. The Federal Power Commission (1974) estimated that the cumulative requirement by the year 2000 will probably amount to between 2.4 and 3.1 million tons of

 which is considerably over the now estimated reserve base of 500,000 tons of economically recoverable uranium. Since this fuel supply is in question, it cannot be considered a viable alternative to hydropower. The quantity of uranium that Amistad power might conserve is not known. The long range solution could be the so called fast breeder reactors, but since these are not now available, they are not a viable alternative.
6.13 No Action. The no action alternative implies that local power consumers can do without additional electrical energy in the face of increasing population. If additional electrical energy is not supplied to people, an increased competition for the present limited supply will result. Lower income groups will become less able to buy power and will suffer a decreased standard of living. If the Amistad power is not provided, the consequence will probably be that additional fossil fuels will be used with resulting air pollution, additional importation of foreign oil, and further depletion of non-renewable domestic oil, gas, and uranium. Acceptance of the no action option would forestall the adverse environmental effects of the construction activities and the pending operation, as well as prevent disruption of the social and economic environment immediately downstream from Amistad Dam.
